The passage also gives desire intentions of its own, working in a direction, rather than treating it as an absence of discipline.

crossReferences.why: States that God does not burden a soul beyond its capacity, the same principle from another angle.
Says no hardship has been placed on this community in religion, closing another passage of instruction.
Opens this sequence with the first stated intention, to make things clear and to guide.

studies.applyIt: Take the demand you place on yourself that you have failed most often, and reduce it deliberately to something you know you can hold. Not as a defeat. The passage says God's own intention is to lighten, and that the creature being addressed was made weak. Consistency at a smaller size is nearer the point than collapse at a larger one.

studies.title: Do Not Consume One Another
studies.meaning: Two things are set side by side with no connective between them, and the commentators read the pairing as deliberate: taking each other's property wrongfully, and killing. The exception given is trade by mutual satisfaction, which makes contentment the dividing line rather than the form of a transaction. The phrase about killing is read two ways in the tradition, as killing one another since a community is one body, and as destroying oneself. Both are preserved.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, opening a short passage on property and life after the long sequence on marriage. Commentators place it in a settled trading community where new arrangements were being worked out and older practices questioned. No single occasion is reported. The address is to believers as a group, and the subject is what members of one community do to each other rather than to outsiders.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to be void or to come to nothing. It names a transaction with no real basis under it, which covers deception and coercion alike without needing to list them.
A reciprocal form from the root for contentment. Both parties must be pleased and not merely agreeing, which sets a standard well above consent obtained under pressure.
The word means a person's own self and also one's own people. That double sense is what allows the classical reading covering both self-destruction and killing within the community.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina's economy ran on face-to-face bargaining, with prices settled by haggling and no fixed rates anywhere. A hard bargain and a fraud could look identical from outside, and disputes over sales were common enough that the market kept its own conventions for settling them. Blood feuds worked at the level of the group, so a single killing pulled in whole families for years.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah moves from commerce to killing inside a single sentence with no transition at all. Commentators note the joining rather than smoothing it over: property taken wrongfully and blood spilled are treated as one category of harm within a community, which is why the closing clause names God's mercy toward the group rather than the individual.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Making mutual satisfaction the criterion puts the moral weight on the state of both parties rather than on the outward form of an agreement, so a contract correctly executed under pressure fails the test. The pairing with killing then establishes a scale: a community's wealth and its lives belong to one order, so that defrauding a member is set beside taking a life.

crossReferences.why: Uses nearly identical wording about consuming property wrongfully, and adds bribing officials to obtain it.
Treats the killing of one person as the killing of all, expanding the logic of this pairing.
States the consequence for doing this in aggression, immediately after the instruction itself.

studies.applyIt: Look at one arrangement you are in where the other party agreed but was not really pleased: a price you pushed, a favour they could not refuse, a deal struck when they had no options. Reopen it this week and offer something back. The standard here is not that they consented. It is that both of you are content.

studies.title: Do Not Covet Another's Share
studies.meaning: The prohibition falls on wishing for what has been given to someone else specifically, not on ambition in general. The commentators keep the distinction: wanting the like of what another has is not what is named here, wanting it taken from them is. Two symmetrical clauses then give men and women each what they have earned, and the sentence redirects the whole impulse outward, telling the listener to ask God for bounty rather than to measure it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, inside a long passage on property, inheritance and household rights. The commentators report an occasion in which women asked about the difference in inheritance shares and in the reward for going out to fight, though the reports vary in their detail. The reply does not adjudicate the comparison. It changes what the questioner is invited to do with the feeling.

keyTerms.note: A verb for wishing something into being, formed from the root for a wish. It describes an inward act rather than a demand, which is why the ayah addresses the imagination before any behaviour.
A portion cut off and set aside, used of a share in an inheritance or of the part of an animal that falls to you. The word assumes a division that has already been made.
A form of the verb for earning that implies deliberate effort towards one's own account. Using it of women and of men in identical clauses gives each the same relation to what they gain.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth in Medina was visible in a way it rarely is now: the number of date palms a family held, the camels in the yard, who ate meat and how often. Neighbours knew each other's holdings down to the tree. In a small oasis town, comparison was not an occasional temptation but the standing condition of daily life, and a family's fortune could turn in a single season.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah gives men and women parallel clauses built from the same verb, one of several places where the Quran states something twice with only the gender changed. Surah 33 does the same at greater length in its thirty-fifth ayah, running ten such pairs in one sentence. The construction is deliberate; Arabic could have used a single plural covering both.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Desire is treated as a thing with a direction rather than a quantity. The passage does not ask for less wanting; it moves the address from the person who has to the God who gave, which converts comparison into request. The closing statement that God knows everything is not a threat here but a reason: the distribution was made by someone with full information, which is exactly what the person comparing lacks.

crossReferences.why: Tells the Prophet not to strain his eyes towards what others have been given to enjoy.
States that God apportions livelihood and raises some above others so they may serve one another.
Describes the same unequal apportioning of provision and turns it towards sharing rather than envy.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you scroll past something that stings, and instead of closing the app, say one specific thing you would want, as a request rather than a comparison. Say it out loud if you can. The ayah does not ask you to stop wanting. It asks you to change who you are addressing.

studies.title: The Widening Circle Of Kindness
studies.meaning: One command about God is followed by a list that moves outward in rings: parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, the near neighbour, the far neighbour, the companion at your side, the traveller, and those your right hands possess. The commentators differ over the near and far neighbour, reading the pair as kinship, as distance, or as shared faith. The list ends not with a further category but with a character, the strutting boaster whom God does not love.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a section on how a household treats those with a claim on it. The ayah follows passages about the property of orphans and precedes warnings about withholding wealth, so it sits inside an argument about money as much as about manners. Classical commentaries record no single occasion for it and read it as a summary statement, one of several places where the surah gathers scattered obligations into one sentence.

keyTerms.note: More than fairness. The root means to do something well and to do it beautifully, so the word asks for a quality of treatment that nobody could demand as a right.
The same root gives the word for a protected person under someone's guarantee. A neighbour in that world was not merely someone nearby; the word carried an implied claim to shelter.

From a root connected with imagination and with horses, describing a person who moves as though watched. It names a bearing rather than a belief, which is why it closes a list about the treatment of others.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Houses in Medina were built wall to wall around shared courtyards, and a family's cooking smoke, quarrels and illnesses were public property. Water came from shared wells, and a household in difficulty could not conceal it for long. The neighbour in this list was a person whose food supply you could see, and the companion at your side has been read as anyone you travel or sit beside for a while.
studies.didYouKnow: The list runs to nine categories, and it moves outward by degrees of closeness rather than by importance: blood, then need, then proximity, then chance. The person you happen to be sitting next to appears in the same sentence as your mother and father, with one single word governing the whole series.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Worship and social conduct are put in one sentence under one verb, which refuses any separation of piety from behaviour towards people. The ordering is itself a claim: obligation weakens with distance but does not stop, and the list keeps going past everyone a tribal society would have recognised as owed anything. Closing with arrogance names the disposition that makes the whole list impossible to keep.

crossReferences.why: Sets out the same widening obligation, beginning with parents and reaching the traveller.
Gives an earlier version of the list as a covenant taken from the Children of Israel.
Uses the same word for strutting, warning against turning one's cheek away from people.

studies.applyIt: Find out one thing this week about a neighbour you would not recognise in a shop. A name, a job, whether they live alone. You are not starting a friendship. The ayah places the person on the other side of your wall in a list with your parents, and learning their name is the smallest way of taking that seriously.

studies.title: Trusts Returned To Their Owners
studies.meaning: Two instructions, addressed to anyone holding something that is not theirs. The first is the return of trusts, which the commentators read broadly: deposits, offices, secrets, anything placed in a person's keeping. The second is judging between people with justice, and it is introduced conditionally, as something that happens when it happens. The phrase set between them, praising the counsel itself, is unusual in the surah and carries warmth rather than warning.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. A widely reported occasion connects the ayah with the key of the Kaaba, handed back to its hereditary keeper after the conquest of Mecca rather than transferred to the new authority. Reports differ over the details, and the commentators note that the wording is general in any case. It sits among passages about authority, dispute, and the handling of what belongs to other people.

keyTerms.note: Plural of a word from the same root as faith and safety. What is deposited with you and what you believe are named by the same consonants, so keeping a trust and being trustworthy are one idea.
From a root for making two things equal in weight. The image is a scale rather than a rulebook, which is why the word covers both fairness between people and the balance of creation.
A compressed exclamation of praise, rare in the Quran. It interrupts the instruction in order to comment on it, so the sentence briefly steps back and admires the counsel it is giving.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca before Islam ran on custodial offices held by families: the key of the sanctuary, the watering of pilgrims, the war banner, the right to convene the assembly. Each was a trust passed down and jealously guarded. Traders also left goods and money with people they would not see for months, on nothing but reputation. Losing a name for trustworthiness ended a man's commercial life.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for trusts shares its root with the word for faith and with the response said after a supplication. The Quran uses the same root at the end of surah 33 for the trust the heavens and the earth declined to carry, so the vocabulary of a deposit left with a neighbour also carries the largest thing said about the human being.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Public and private integrity are given a single vocabulary. The ayah moves from the small deposit to judgement between parties without changing verbs, so the qualities required in a courtroom are the ones already exercised over a borrowed tool. Naming God as hearing and seeing at the close is precise rather than decorative: the two failures in view are things said and things done behind closed doors.

crossReferences.why: Warns against betraying trusts knowingly, using the same word in a Medinan setting.
Uses the same root for the trust offered to the heavens and the earth and carried by humanity.
Repeats the demand for just judgement, adding that hatred must not push you off it.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you are holding that belongs to someone else: a borrowed book, a password, a piece of information told to you in confidence. Return one of them this week, or check that you are still keeping it the way its owner would want. The ayah begins with objects and moves to judgement, in that order.

studies.title: When You Disagree, Refer It Back
studies.meaning: The verb for obedience is repeated for God and for the Messenger but not for those in authority, and the commentators read that omission as deliberate: obedience to human authority is attached to the first two rather than standing on its own. Then the harder half. Disputes are to be referred back, and the condition attached is belief in God and the Last Day, so willingness to be corrected is presented as the test of the claim to believe.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a stretch dealing with authority, arbitration and conflict inside the community. Reports connect the ayah with a dispute over a commander appointed for an expedition, though the details vary and the commentators do not settle them. Medina at this time was a settlement of formerly rival clans newly living under a single arrangement, where the question of who decides was live and unresolved.

keyTerms.note: Literally the possessors of the matter. The commentators read it of those entrusted with command and of those with knowledge, and the phrase is left broad rather than tied to any office.
A verb for returning something to where it came from, used of giving back a borrowed item. The dispute is treated as a thing to be handed over rather than a position to be argued.
From a root meaning to return to an origin. It covers both the interpretation of something and how it turns out in the end, so the closing praise concerns consequences as much as meaning.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian disputes were settled by arbitration rather than by courts. Two parties agreed on a judge, often a respected outsider, and accepted his ruling because both had chosen him. There was no enforcement beyond honour and pressure. Referring a quarrel to an agreed authority was therefore a familiar procedure; what changed was the identity of the arbitrator and the fact that neither side got to pick.
studies.didYouKnow: Classical commentaries treat this as one of the central ayat on governance, and part of the reason is grammatical. The verb for obeying is stated twice and then dropped before those in authority, which in Arabic joins them to the Messenger's clause rather than giving them a clause of their own. A great deal was built on that single omission.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Authority is granted and limited in the same sentence. Something is owed to those who carry responsibility, and the grammar keeps that owing derivative rather than original. The passage also treats disagreement as expected rather than shameful, supplying a procedure for it instead of a prohibition. The final phrase makes that procedure a practical claim: this way of settling things actually ends better, not only more properly.

crossReferences.why: Sharpens the same point, that accepting the Messenger's judgement without resistance is the mark of faith.
States that whatever people differ in, its judgement rests with God.
Places consultation before decision, which is the other half of how authority is described.

studies.applyIt: In your next disagreement, before you answer, say what the other person's position is until they agree that you have it right. It costs a minute. The ayah's procedure begins with taking a dispute out of your own hands, and there is no smaller version of that than letting someone else define what is being argued about.

studies.title: Excellent Are Those Companions
studies.meaning: A hard section about people who would not accept arbitration ends with an invitation rather than a threat. Four ranks are named: prophets, the utterly truthful, the witnesses, and the upright. What is promised is not a rank but company, being with them. The commentators note that the promise is made to whoever obeys, without any qualification of degree, so the lowest of the four is not set as a ceiling for the ordinary person.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The ayat just before these describe people who claimed belief while seeking judgement elsewhere, and what they would have been given had they done otherwise. Classical sources preserve a report of a companion who grieved that death would separate him from the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), and record it alongside the flow of the surrounding argument.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form from the root for truth, describing someone whose truthfulness is habitual rather than occasional. The same title is given elsewhere in the Quran to Abraham, to Joseph and to Mary.
The word covers both giving testimony and dying for a cause, and the commentators read it in both senses here. Its underlying meaning is presence: a witness is one who was there.
A word for the person you travel alongside, from a root for gentleness and ease. It is singular in the Arabic though the company named is plural, which reads as one shared companionship.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Travel in Arabia was done in company because it could not safely be done alone. Choosing a companion for a journey was a serious decision, and proverbs about it survive: pick the companion before the road. A bad one could rob you, abandon you at a well, or simply make a month of walking unbearable. The word used here for company is the travelling one.
studies.didYouKnow: The four groups named here are the ones classical commentators identify with the people asked about in the opening surah, whose path is requested in every unit of prayer. Reading the two passages together makes this ayah the answer to a request that most Muslims make more often than any other sentence they say.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Reward is described as relationship rather than as property. The four categories are not merged, so distinctions of rank remain real, but the promise crosses them: the ordinary believer is placed with the prophets rather than at a respectful distance below them. That moves the goal of a religious life away from accumulation and towards belonging, which the closing word makes explicit by choosing the language of travel.

crossReferences.why: Asks for the path of those favoured, whom this passage then names.
Calls those who believe in God and His messengers the truthful and the witnesses.
States the condition these ayat reward, accepting the Messenger's judgement without resistance.

studies.applyIt: Think about who you spend your unstructured hours with, the people whose opinions you find yourself repeating without having decided to. Name three of them. The ayah makes company the reward, which suggests company is also the method, and the honest question is whether your current one is taking you where you say you want to go.

studies.title: Good From God, Harm From Yourself
studies.meaning: Attribution is divided asymmetrically, and the commentators are careful about what the ayah does not say. Everything remains under God's decree; the point is where the human being should look. Good is received, so it points outward. Harm is traced to one's own doing, so it points inward. The second ayah then removes the messenger from enforcement entirely: obeying him counts as obeying God, but refusal is not his to prevent.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following ayat describing people who attributed their misfortunes to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and their good fortune to themselves. The commentators read this passage as answering that habit directly, and the reverse at Uhud had given it a recent and concrete instance. The surah at this point is largely occupied with people who kept a distance from the community while claiming to belong to it.

keyTerms.note: A verb for a thing hitting its mark, used of an arrow finding its target and of rain reaching land. It presents both good and harm as arriving rather than as being produced.
The word covers a good deed and a good happening, both a kindness done and a piece of fortune received. That breadth is why the ayah can move between morality and circumstance without changing terms.
One who preserves and watches over something, used of guarding property and of memorising. Denying this role to the messenger limits his responsibility to delivery rather than to results.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabs before Islam read fortune in omens: the direction a startled bird flew, the day a journey began, the person met on the road. Bad luck attached itself to people, and a newcomer whose arrival coincided with drought could be blamed for it. Holding a stranger responsible for a failed harvest was ordinary reasoning, and the surah is answering people who did exactly that in Medina.
studies.didYouKnow: The two halves of this ayah were debated at length by the classical commentators precisely because they seem to sit awkwardly with the ayah just before, which says everything is from God. The resolution given across the major commentaries is that the earlier statement describes causation while this one describes responsibility, two different questions asked of the same event.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Credit and blame are assigned in the direction least flattering to the self, which reverses the usual human accounting. That single reversal does two things at once: it protects gratitude from becoming self-congratulation, and it keeps misfortune from turning into a grievance against God. The second ayah adds a limit on religious authority. The messenger is owed obedience and is not given custody of anyone's outcome.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle about misfortune, adding that much is pardoned.
Traces every blessing to God and describes the cry for help when harm touches.
Repeats the limit on the messenger's role, a reminder and not a controller.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing that went wrong for you recently and write the shortest honest sentence about your own part in it. Not a confession, an inventory. Then take one thing that went right and name someone or something outside yourself that made it possible. Do both, in that order, and notice which one was harder.

studies.title: A Word Spoken For Someone
studies.meaning: Intercession here is not the Day of Judgement kind. It is the everyday act of speaking on someone's behalf, and the ayah gives it weight in both directions: a share of the good you enabled, a portion of the harm. Then a smaller instance of the same principle. A greeting arrives and is to be answered with a better one or at least returned, so even the minimum is defined. Both ayat close with a divine name about counting.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a passage about who stands with whom in a divided situation. The commentators record no specific occasion. What they note is the placement: these two ayat sit between hard material about people who would not commit themselves, and they describe the small transactions by which a community actually holds together, put in the same register as the larger loyalties around them.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to make something even by adding a second to it. The intercessor joins himself to the person he speaks for, which is why he then shares in the result.
A word connected with the pad placed on a camel's back so a second rider can sit behind. It is chosen for the bad share, rather than the plainer word used for the good one.
From the root for life. The standard greeting was a wish for life, so returning one better than you received means adding to what somebody has just wished you.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Access in that society ran through intercession. A man wanting a debt forgiven, a captive released or a marriage agreed sent someone with standing to speak for him, and the speaker's reputation travelled with the request. Refusing an intercessor was a public act. Greetings worked the same way, marking whether a person stood inside your circle, and passing someone in silence was a recognised form of hostility.
studies.didYouKnow: The second ayah sets both a floor and a ceiling for a greeting: better than the one received, or exactly equal to it. The Quran rarely specifies a courtesy this precisely, and the classical commentaries note that the equal return is named as the lower limit rather than as the expected response.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Speech is treated as participation. A word said on someone's behalf makes the speaker a party to what follows, so influence is never neutral and cannot be disowned afterwards. The greeting then extends the same logic to the smallest social act available. Nothing here is too minor to be counted, and both ayat close with divine names drawn from accounting rather than from mercy or power.

crossReferences.why: Instructs the Prophet to open with peace when believers come to him, the same greeting.
Makes peace the greeting exchanged in the Garden, the same word used here.
Praises private talk that urges charity, kindness or reconciliation between people.

studies.applyIt: Answer the next message you receive with slightly more than you were given: one extra sentence, a question back, a name at the start. It takes seconds. The ayah sets returning the same as the floor and going beyond it as the expectation, and most of what makes a person feel met is exactly that small margin.

studies.title: Whoever Wrongs His Own Soul
studies.meaning: Two conditional sentences with different subjects. The first begins with a wrong done and ends, with no interval, in finding God forgiving. Nothing is placed between the seeking and the finding. The commentators note the verb: the person does not so much receive forgiveness as discover that it was already the case. The second sentence closes off a natural evasion by saying the sin is earned against oneself, so nobody else carries it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following a passage about someone who committed a theft and tried to shift the blame onto an innocent man. The commentators report the case in detail, though accounts of the names and circumstances differ. These two ayat are the general conclusion drawn from it: the door back is open, and moving a wrong onto another person is precisely what the surrounding ayat have just refused.

keyTerms.note: The root means to put something where it does not belong, and it also gives the word for darkness. Wrongdoing is described as misplacement, and the first party damaged is the one who does it.
A verb of discovery rather than of receiving. It suggests the forgiveness was there to be found, and that the seeking is what brings a person to where it already was.
Commercial vocabulary for gain made through effort. Applying it to sin makes wrongdoing something worked for and accumulated, held in an account belonging to whoever did the work.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Guilt in a clan society was rarely private. A theft attached to a whole family, and blood money for a killing was raised across the kin group, so wrongdoing was distributed by default. The pressure to push blame outward onto an outsider or a weaker household was practical rather than merely dishonest. These ayat cut against a settlement that everyone listening understood from the inside.
studies.didYouKnow: The pairing of divine names at the end of each ayah is doing work. The first closes with forgiving and merciful, the second with knowing and wise, so the sentence that offers pardon and the sentence that assigns responsibility are sealed with different attributes. Matching the closing names to the content is a consistent feature of these Medinan passages.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Forgiveness is described as available before it is asked for, which changes what asking is. The person is not persuading God but locating something. At the same time the second ayah refuses to let mercy blur responsibility: a wrong stays attached to whoever did it, and cannot be transferred to a scapegoat or absorbed by a group. Openness and accountability are stated in adjacent sentences without any tension.

crossReferences.why: Extends the same offer at its widest, addressing those who have wronged themselves greatly.
States that no bearer of burdens carries the burden of another.
Continues the passage, describing the person who throws his own fault onto someone innocent.

studies.applyIt: Think of a fault you have always narrated with a reason attached, the version where circumstances or another person explain most of it. Try telling it once, silently, without the explanation. The ayah puts nothing between asking and finding, and the thing that usually stands in the way is the account we have practised.

studies.title: Witnesses Even Against Yourselves
studies.meaning: The demand is not to be just but to be one who stands up with justice, a form describing a posture maintained rather than an act performed. The hard cases are then named in order of difficulty: yourself, your parents, your relatives. A second temptation is anticipated, the pull towards whichever party seems more deserving of sympathy, and it is refused by saying God is nearer to both. The obstacle identified is desire, not ignorance.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the same section that dealt with a theft blamed on an innocent man, where the community's instinct had been to protect one of its own. The commentators read this ayah as generalising from that episode. Medina was a town of clans in which testimony was routinely shaped by loyalty, and an oath sworn for a kinsman was closer to a duty than to a lie.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form from the verb to stand, describing a standing role rather than a single stand. The same word is used of maintaining prayer, so it carries the sense of upholding something continuously.
A word tied to portions and shares, so the justice named is the kind that divides things fairly. Its own root can also carry deviation, and the form used here reverses that sense.
From a root for falling and for empty air. It names the pull of what one wants, pictured as a descent, which is why the ayah treats it as the thing that makes testimony swerve.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Justice in Arabia was tribal arithmetic. A killing was answered by a killing from the other clan, and a man who testified against his own people had cut the branch he sat on: protection, marriage prospects and trade all ran through kin. There was no state to appeal to if your family disowned you. Standing as a witness against a relative was nearer to exile than to inconvenience.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran states this demand twice with its terms reversed. Here justice is the thing stood up for and God is the one witnessed to; at 5:8 the standing is for God and the witnessing is done with justice. The commentators note the mirroring, and the second passage names a different obstacle, hatred rather than desire.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Justice is grounded in something other than social benefit. The witness testifies to God, which makes accuracy a form of worship and removes the question of who is helped by the answer. The clause about rich and poor is the sharpest part: sympathy for the weak is no licence to bend a fact, and neither is deference to the strong. God is said to be nearer to both parties than the witness is.

crossReferences.why: States the same demand with the terms reversed, and names hatred as the pressure to resist.
Requires that speech be just even when a relative is involved.
Warns the Prophet against arguing for the treacherous, in the episode behind this passage.

studies.applyIt: The next time you retell an argument you were part of, include the strongest thing the other person said, in their words rather than your summary of it. You are not conceding anything. The ayah begins with testimony against yourself, and the smallest version of that is refusing to edit someone else's case when nobody would notice.

studies.title: Believe In All Of It
studies.meaning: The address is to people who already believe, and the command is to believe. The commentators offer a range: stay firm on it, deepen it, or accept what you have not yet acknowledged. The content is then listed as a chain, this Book and the Book sent before it, and the denial clause widens to angels, messengers and the Last Day. What is described is not a set of separate beliefs but one thing with parts, which is why rejecting any of them is called straying far.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a surah much concerned with people whose commitment was partial and with argument between communities holding earlier scriptures. The insistence on the Book sent before is not incidental in that setting. The commentators record no single occasion and read the address as directed at the community itself, whose belief was being asked to become something more than a stated position.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form suggesting descent in stages, used of the Quran's revelation over years. A plainer form appears in the same sentence for the earlier scripture, and the commentators note the difference.
Classical grammarians connect the word with a root for a message or an errand. Angels appear in the list of what may not be rejected, placed between God Himself and the scriptures He sent.
The verb for losing your road in open country where there are no landmarks. It is paired here with a word for distance, so error is measured as a length walked rather than a single wrong turn.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina was a town where scriptural religion was already familiar. Jewish tribes had lived there for generations, kept their books, and their scholars were consulted about the past. Arabs in the oasis had grown up hearing of earlier prophets and of one still expected. A claim to continue that line was intelligible to everybody there in a way it had not been in Mecca.
studies.didYouKnow: Five things are named here as objects of belief, and the same five are gathered in the long ayah on righteousness in surah 2, where it is defined as belief in God, the Last Day, the angels, the Book and the prophets. The order differs between the two, and neither passage presents its list as exhaustive.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Belief is presented as something that can be commanded of believers, which means it is not treated as a state already completed. The list refuses a religion beginning with this messenger: earlier scripture is part of the content rather than a courtesy extended to others. And the closing image measures rejection as distance travelled, which implies that positions are arrived at gradually and can be walked back.

crossReferences.why: Gathers the same objects of belief, defining righteousness by them rather than by direction of prayer.
Shows the response, believers making no distinction between any of His messengers.
Names the same religion as enjoined on Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus alike.

studies.applyIt: Pick one of the things you say you believe and ask what you did about it this month. Not whether you affirmed it, what you did. The ayah addresses people who had already said the words and asks them for the thing itself, which suggests the gap between saying and holding is normal rather than a scandal.
